title: "Low-Rank Adaptation"

term: "Low-Rank Adaptation"

## Simple explanation

Low-rank adaptation is a way to customize a pretrained model by learning a
compact update instead of changing every original weight. LoRA (Low-Rank
Adaptation) is the best-known method using this idea.

## Technical explanation

For a frozen weight matrix $W_0$, an adapted matrix can be represented as:

$$
W = W_0 + BA
$$

The trainable matrices $A$ and $B$ are chosen so their shared inner dimension,
the rank $r$, is much smaller than the dimensions of $W_0$. This constrains
the update to a lower-dimensional parameterization. LoRA typically includes
an additional scale factor and initializes the factors so the initial update
is zero or near zero.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Low-rank adaptation can make model customization more resource-efficient and
make it practical to maintain separate task or customer adapters. The
trade-offs include adapter quality, rank selection, compatibility, and the
serving cost of loading or applying adapters.

## How it works

The method inserts a low-rank trainable path alongside selected frozen
weights. Fine-tuning updates the path's factors based on the task objective.
When appropriate, the resulting update can be merged into the original
weights; otherwise, it can be applied as a separate adapter.

## Practical example

A research group can adapt the same base language model for summarization and
question answering using separate low-rank adapters. Each adapter stores a
compact task-specific update, while the base model remains shared.

## Common misconceptions

- Low-rank adaptation describes a family of techniques; LoRA is a specific and widely used approach.
- The method does not eliminate the need to select training data, tune settings, and evaluate the adapted model.
- Lower parameter count does not imply that every runtime or serving cost is reduced by the same amount.
